## Answer

**Not necessarily.** The hypotheses do not force the union to be countably generated, nor do they force it to be non‑countably‑generated. The union can be either. The nontrivial part is refuting the natural conjecture "the union of a chain of non‑countably‑generated ideals is again non‑countably‑generated": I give a counterexample in which the union **is** countably generated.

(The opposite direction is trivial: a one‑element chain $\{J\}$ with $J$ non‑countably‑generated has union $J$, which is not countably generated.)

---

### Counterexample: a chain of non‑countably‑generated ideals with countably generated union

Let
\[
\mathfrak A=\mathcal P(\omega\times\omega_{1}),
\]
and write $C_{n}=\{n\}\times\omega_{1}$ for the $n$‑th "column" ($n\in\omega$). Each $C_{n}$ is in bijection with $\omega_{1}$.

**The candidate union.** Define
\[
I=\big\langle C_{n}:n\in\omega\big\rangle_{\mathrm{id}}
   =\big\{X\subseteq\omega\times\omega_{1}:\pi_{1}[X]\text{ is finite}\big\}.
\]
This is the ideal of sets supported on finitely many columns. It is generated by the countable family $\{C_{n}:n\in\omega\}$, so **$I$ is countably generated**.

**The chain.** For $n\in\omega$ set
\[
J_{n}=\Big\{X\in I:\text{ for every }m\ge n,\; X\cap C_{m}\text{ is countable}\Big\}.
\]
In words: $J_{n}$ consists of those elements of $I$ which, on columns $C_{m}$ with $m\ge n$, meet each column only countably (columns $C_{0},\dots,C_{n-1}$ may be met arbitrarily).

*$J_{n}$ is an ideal.* $\emptyset\in J_{n}$; if $X\in J_{n}$ and $Y\subseteq X$ then $Y\cap C_{m}\subseteq X\cap C_{m}$ is countable for $m\ge n$ and $\pi_{1}[Y]\subseteq\pi_{1}[X]$ is finite, so $Y\in J_{n}$; and if $X,Y\in J_{n}$ then $(X\cup Y)\cap C_{m}=(X\cap C_{m})\cup(Y\cap C_{m})$ is countable for $m\ge n$ and $\pi_{1}[X\cup Y]$ is finite, so $X\cup Y\in J_{n}$.

*The chain is increasing.* If $X\in J_{n}$ then $X\cap C_{m}$ is countable for all $m\ge n$, hence certainly for all $m\ge n+1$; so $X\in J_{n+1}$. Thus $J_{0}\subseteq J_{1}\subseteq\cdots$.

*The union equals $I$.* The inclusion $J_{n}\subseteq I$ is immediate from the definition. Conversely, take $X\in I$ and let $\pi_{1}[X]=\{i_{1},\dots,i_{k}\}$, finite. Put $N=\max\{i_{1},\dots,i_{k}\}+1$. For every $m\ge N$ we have $m>\max i_{j}$, so $X\cap C_{m}=\emptyset$, which is countable. Hence $X\in J_{N}$. Therefore
\[
\bigcup_{n\in\omega}J_{n}=I.
\]

*Each $J_{n}$ is **not** countably generated.* Suppose, for a contradiction, that $J_{n}=\langle \{G_{p}:p\in\omega\}\rangle_{\mathrm{id}}$ for some countable family $\{G_{p}\}\subseteq J_{n}$. Since each $G_{p}\in J_{n}$ and $n\ge n$, the intersection $G_{p}\cap C_{n}$ is countable. Set
\[
B=\bigcup_{p\in\omega}(G_{p}\cap C_{n})\subseteq C_{n}.
\]
Then $B$ is countable (a countable union of countable sets), while $C_{n}\cong\omega_{1}$ is uncountable, so there exists $d\in C_{n}\setminus B$. Now $\{d\}\in J_{n}$: indeed $\pi_{1}[\{d\}]=\{n\}$ is finite, and $\{d\}\cap C_{m}$ is $\{d\}$ (countable) when $m=n$ and $\emptyset$ when $m\neq n$, hence countable for every $m\ge n$. On the other hand, $d\notin B\supseteq G_{p}\cap C_{n}$ and $d\in C_{n}$, so $d\notin G_{p}$ for every $p$; consequently $d\notin\bigcup_{p}G_{p}$, and therefore $\{d\}$ is not contained in any finite union $G_{p_{1}}\cup\cdots\cup G_{p_{k}}$. But every element of the ideal generated by $\{G_{p}\}$ is contained in such a finite union. Hence $\{d\}\notin\langle\{G_{p}\}\rangle$, contradicting $\{d\}\in J_{n}$. So $J_{n}$ is not countably generated.

---

### Conclusion

We have produced a Boolean algebra $\mathfrak A=\mathcal P(\omega\times\omega_{1})$ and an increasing chain $\mathfrak J=\{J_{n}:n\in\omega\}$ of ideals, **none of them countably generated**, whose union $\bigcup\mathfrak J=I$ **is countably generated** (by $\{C_{n}:n\in\omega\}$). Together with the trivial observation that a singleton chain $\{J\}$ with $J$ non‑countably‑generated yields a non‑countably‑generated union, this shows:

**The union $\bigcup\mathfrak J$ is not determined to be countably generated or not by the stated hypotheses; it can be either.** In particular, the answer to the question "Is the union countably generated?" is **not necessarily**.

## Answer

**Not necessarily.** The hypotheses do not force the union to be countably generated, nor do they force it to be non‑countably‑generated. The union can be either. The nontrivial part is refuting the natural conjecture "the union of a chain of non‑countably‑generated ideals is again non‑countably‑generated": I give a counterexample in which the union **is** countably generated.

(The opposite direction is trivial: a one‑element chain $\{J\}$ with $J$ non‑countably‑generated has union $J$, which is not countably generated.)

---

### Counterexample: a chain of non‑countably‑generated ideals with countably generated union

Let
\[
\mathfrak A=\mathcal P(\omega\times\omega_{1}),
\]
and write $C_{n}=\{n\}\times\omega_{1}$ for the $n$‑th "column" ($n\in\omega$). Each $C_{n}$ is in bijection with $\omega_{1}$.

**The candidate union.** Define
\[
I=\big\langle C_{n}:n\in\omega\big\rangle_{\mathrm{id}}
   =\big\{X\subseteq\omega\times\omega_{1}:\pi_{1}[X]\text{ is finite}\big\}.
\]
This is the ideal of sets supported on finitely many columns. It is generated by the countable family $\{C_{n}:n\in\omega\}$, so **$I$ is countably generated**.

**The chain.** For $n\in\omega$ set
\[
J_{n}=\Big\{X\in I:\text{ for every }m\ge n,\; X\cap C_{m}\text{ is countable}\Big\}.
\]
In words: $J_{n}$ consists of those elements of $I$ which, on columns $C_{m}$ with $m\ge n$, meet each column only countably (columns $C_{0},\dots,C_{n-1}$ may be met arbitrarily).

*$J_{n}$ is an ideal.* $\emptyset\in J_{n}$; if $X\in J_{n}$ and $Y\subseteq X$ then $Y\cap C_{m}\subseteq X\cap C_{m}$ is countable for $m\ge n$ and $\pi_{1}[Y]\subseteq\pi_{1}[X]$ is finite, so $Y\in J_{n}$; and if $X,Y\in J_{n}$ then $(X\cup Y)\cap C_{m}=(X\cap C_{m})\cup(Y\cap C_{m})$ is countable for $m\ge n$ and $\pi_{1}[X\cup Y]$ is finite, so $X\cup Y\in J_{n}$.

*The chain is increasing.* If $X\in J_{n}$ then $X\cap C_{m}$ is countable for all $m\ge n$, hence certainly for all $m\ge n+1$; so $X\in J_{n+1}$. Thus $J_{0}\subseteq J_{1}\subseteq\cdots$.

*The union equals $I$.* The inclusion $J_{n}\subseteq I$ is immediate from the definition. Conversely, take $X\in I$ and let $\pi_{1}[X]=\{i_{1},\dots,i_{k}\}$, finite. Put $N=\max\{i_{1},\dots,i_{k}\}+1$. For every $m\ge N$ we have $m>\max i_{j}$, so $X\cap C_{m}=\emptyset$, which is countable. Hence $X\in J_{N}$. Therefore
\[
\bigcup_{n\in\omega}J_{n}=I.
\]

*Each $J_{n}$ is **not** countably generated.* Suppose, for a contradiction, that $J_{n}=\langle \{G_{p}:p\in\omega\}\rangle_{\mathrm{id}}$ for some countable family $\{G_{p}\}\subseteq J_{n}$. Since each $G_{p}\in J_{n}$ and $n\ge n$, the intersection $G_{p}\cap C_{n}$ is countable. Set
\[
B=\bigcup_{p\in\omega}(G_{p}\cap C_{n})\subseteq C_{n}.
\]
Then $B$ is countable (a countable union of countable sets), while $C_{n}\cong\omega_{1}$ is uncountable, so there exists $d\in C_{n}\setminus B$. Now $\{d\}\in J_{n}$: indeed $\pi_{1}[\{d\}]=\{n\}$ is finite, and $\{d\}\cap C_{m}$ is $\{d\}$ (countable) when $m=n$ and $\emptyset$ when $m\neq n$, hence countable for every $m\ge n$. On the other hand, $d\notin B\supseteq G_{p}\cap C_{n}$ and $d\in C_{n}$, so $d\notin G_{p}$ for every $p$; consequently $d\notin\bigcup_{p}G_{p}$, and therefore $\{d\}$ is not contained in any finite union $G_{p_{1}}\cup\cdots\cup G_{p_{k}}$. But every element of the ideal generated by $\{G_{p}\}$ is contained in such a finite union. Hence $\{d\}\notin\langle\{G_{p}\}\rangle$, contradicting $\{d\}\in J_{n}$. So $J_{n}$ is not countably generated.

---

### Conclusion

We have produced a Boolean algebra $\mathfrak A=\mathcal P(\omega\times\omega_{1})$ and an increasing chain $\mathfrak J=\{J_{n}:n\in\omega\}$ of ideals, **none of them countably generated**, whose union $\bigcup\mathfrak J=I$ **is countably generated** (by $\{C_{n}:n\in\omega\}$). Together with the trivial observation that a singleton chain $\{J\}$ with $J$ non‑countably‑generated yields a non‑countably‑generated union, this shows:

**The union $\bigcup\mathfrak J$ is not determined to be countably generated or not by the stated hypotheses; it can be either.** In particular, the answer to the question "Is the union countably generated?" is **not necessarily**.
